utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. Defence teams are missing only Ms. Condon, as stated by Mr. Zivanovic, as explained by Mr. Zivanovic. And also I see Mr. Bourgon absent today. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: She is coming tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Mr. Bourgon, I suppose, will be with us soon as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. He's in the office working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer in the back, no others behind the column. Please take a seat. I will come to you very soon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we did get your message, Mr. Josse; however I don't think there will be need for any further submissions considering what we are going to decide now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we went through the entire proceedings yesterday dealing with the submission, oral submission of Madam Fauveau to which all the other Defence teams associated themselves. It is a fair statement that we would like to make, and namely that we are broadly satisfied that the Prosecution is endeavoring to comply with our directives considering also the current circumstances. We do, however, once more enjoin the Prosecution to continue to do so. We also wish to state that generally we accept that there is bound to be some irrelevant material in such statements as the present one, especially when one considers that this statement and others like it may have been given or indeed were given for the purposes of other trials too. In the particular case that we have before us it is difficult for the Trial Chamber to establish a priori that everything that the defence teams deem to be irrelevant is indeed irrelevant. As a result we feel that denying the Prosecution request to convert Witness 45 to a 92 ter witness is the best way to proceed forward in this particular instance, and that is our decision. So you will produce this witness viva voce. Not this witness, Witness 45. Now, I come to you, sir. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wish to welcome you to this Tribunal where you will soon start giving evidence. Our rules require that before your -- you start testifying you make a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand to you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey will be putting some questions to you. He will then be followed on cross-examination by the various Defence teams. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you tell us your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Zlatan Celanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: In Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where do you -- did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: In Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you still live in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just briefly, what kind of law do you practice in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Property law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to take you back to the war years, and specifically the year -- just roughly 1995, at first. Can you tell us what your position was in 1995 in the -- in the army?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I was an officer for legal affairs, religious affairs, and moral guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what unit?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: That was with the headquarters, the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Bratunac Brigade, light infantry Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Major Ratko Jeftic, assistant commander within the same organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And his commander for July 1995 was who?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Commander Vidoje Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your duties were in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. My duties were, within my regular activities, to institute proceedings against soldiers, conscripts, who violated disciplinary rules. Do you need any elaboration on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Besides disciplinary rules, did that include criminal -- criminal violations?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I was not competent to initiate criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever investigate or help oversee an investigation of when a -- when a soldier committed some sort of crime, whether it be assault or theft?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But that was within the disciplinary action or proceedings, I would take a statement from the offender and then we would decide whether that was a crime or a disciplinary infraction and I had to report to the commander on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who would you get your commands from to initiate an interview for an offender or an investigation like this?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: From the commander. Always from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to July 1995 specifically. And I want to go to the time of about the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. Now, I know you've testified before that you weren't real good with the dates; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So I want to -- I'll ask you questions around time -- incidents or -- or things that -- that happened that -- that may help you recall roughly what time-frame it is. So my -- the first thing I want to ask you about is let's go to the day -- wasn't -- was there a day when you were at your office and some Muslim prisoners were brought by your office that you did interviews of?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us where your office was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the building where the military police was housed, or rather the military police platoon. That was a building near the headquarters building, but not sharing the same yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And that -- that headquarters building, can you just roughly describe it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I can. The building of the brigade headquarters was actually -- was actually a factory building of Kaolin, and in the premises of that building the headquarters of the brigade, that is to say various organs and the commander, were housed. And that was behind the building where I had my office, in another yard, some 30 to 50 metres away. If you need additional details, I will be happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's okay. I think there's some familiarity with that. So tell us about when those prisoners were brought by. Roughly when did that happen on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning hours at around 10.00, 11.00. Around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Prior to those prisoners coming by, had any senior officers spoken to you about any subject related to interviews or prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when had Mr. Beara spoken to you about this subject?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. It was either on the 12th in the evening or on Monday in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say -- sorry, I think we spoke at the same time by accident. We didn't get your last answer.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was either in the evening on the 12th of July or in the morning on the 13th of July. I'm not sure, I can't remember, but we had two meetings in those two days and the first one was either in the evening on the 12th or 13th in the morning, and the second one was on the 13th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And had you met Mr. Beara prior to the -- the date you had that meeting with him that we're talking about now?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier, yes. In 1994, in 1993, on various occasions when he came to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just -- just roughly tell us when he came to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, what was he doing, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what he did, but I guess he came to inspect security organs, to see Nikolic or some similar matters. I never discussed the reason of his visit with him. It wasn't appropriate for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say Nikolic, do you mean Momir Nikolic, the chief of security and intelligence of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, what was Mr. Beara's rank?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. He is either a colonel or lieutenant-colonel. I apologise, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, can I know the rank of the witness at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, when you were the -- you held that position, did you have a rank in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what was -- what was your level in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I did my professional tasks because I'm qualified professionally, but I hold no rank.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the first sentence the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We didn't quite hear the first part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, the interpreters couldn't hear the first part of your answer. If you could repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a rank. I was an ordinary soldier holding no rank. As for the post that I held, I was hired or engaged because I'm a qualified lawyer, and because somebody holding that degree was qualified for that post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused. One time the witness said he was an officer, and now he says -- he is saying he was an ordinary soldier. Could you clarify with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It may be the same word in the language, my colleague advises me, so I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have a little translation issue, but let me just try to clarify it. Have you ever said you were an officer in the -- in the VRS as in a lieutenant, major, of that rank or higher?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Never. Because I'm not an officer. I was a "referent" which can be translated as a desk officer. This is a post I held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to Mr. Beara, when you saw him, where was it that you saw him this first time, either the night of the 12th or the morning of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: In front of the military police building in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what if anything did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: He asked me how I was, what I was doing, in those days, and I told him the usual tasks, believing that he knew what my usual tasks were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what else did he say?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: He said "fine," and then he asked me whether I had any information on the people who had sinned in relation to the Serbian people. Or rather, information on the people who we suspected had torched Serbian villages, killed civilians and referring to the Muslims. And I told him that this was all documented in a book.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the name of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of the book slowly? We didn't quite hear it all.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The name of the book is The Chronicle of Our Cemetery. The author is Milivoje Ivanisevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Beara use the word "sinned," in a -- sinned, religious context, or is that your word?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the sense of committing crimes against the Serbs in previous years in relation to that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. When you told him about the book, what else was mentioned, if anything?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that it would be good for me to ask for IDs from people who were brought to the police building or taken into custody by them and brought there just to check whether anybody mentioned in that book was among them. And if that was the case, to inform one of the security organs that such a person was there, so that action could be taken so that the case could be forwarded to the competent prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And at the time he -- he said that, had anybody been brought by your office yet, any Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So now let's go back to the -- what you've described as the morning of the 13th. When you say some Muslims were -- were brought by your office, can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: A group of five or six Muslims arrived in a vehicle escorted by soldiers who were referred to as members of special forces in conversation with the military police. So I assumed that they were members of special forces or special military police forces. They came there and asked about the location of the school building, the elementary school building, so they could take these people there. So the military policemen who were there in front of the building explained to them, gave them directions, pointed. And I approached them, telling them that I would need to ID these people, telling them why I would need to do that, and I told them to wait a little bit before taking them elsewhere, which they accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us the military policemen that gave these -- these special soldiers or forces that you have described, did you know what unit the military policemen were from?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were not from the Bratunac Brigade, because they were completely unfamiliar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were they part of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Most likely, yes. They couldn't have appeared there otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was a prisoner brought to you that you knew?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Resid Sinanovic, a colleague of mine from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was he brought to you with these other six, I think you said Muslims? Was he brought to you at the same time as those six?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. There were six or seven of them, roughly. But within five or 10 minutes -- he wasn't brought with them. He came with Captain Mirnikovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of the officer that Resid Sinanovic came with?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, we had just an understandable translation glitch on the first name. All right. And was Mr. Beara around at the time that these Muslims were brought to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what if anything did Momir Nikolic say to you when you brought you Resid Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: He brought him into the office without me seeing that because I was outside. And then he found me in the yard in front of the building and said to me, "I brought in your colleague, Resid Sinanovic, and he is right now in your office sitting there." Should I tell you the rest of what he said to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: And then he said to me that I should check the circumstances because Resid was also mentioned in the book, The Chronicle of Our Cemetery, among other people, as somebody who was suspected of having participated in the attack on the village of Bjelovac. He said we should check the paperwork to see whether there was any statement concerning this and that I should talk to Resid about it to see if that was true or not. Following that he said good-bye to Resid, shook hands with him, went out, and I never saw him again. I'm referring to Nikolic. He said something similar to what Mr. Beara said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing special. I walked into the office and I started talking to Resid. It was a normal dialogue. I talked to him as one would talk to a colleague. We hadn't seen each other in a while throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was -- what was Mr. Sinanovic's profession?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you -- did you -- take notes during your -- your talk with him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you just -- I'll show you those notes a little later, but can you just briefly tell us what -- what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: After we greeted each other, as people would, I told him that it was a good thing that he was there, that I see him, that there were some indications to the effect of survivors from Bjelovac after the torching of the village and the killing of many civilians suspected him of having taken part in that attack. Not only he, but his wife as well, which was a bit unusual or rather absurd. Women did not wage war then in that part of the world. He said, "Colleague, never mind, you tell me everything you have to say. My conscience is clear, and I wasn't even close to Bjelovac when all of that happened." I had copies of some unreliable statements. Some elderly women from Bjelovac had said that they had recognised Resid Sinanovic's voice in the woods, and when I asked how far away the woods were from the house, 600 to 700 metres, perhaps even up to 1 kilometre, which is impossible to recognise anybody's voice at that distance. You could not recognise your own child's voice let alone -- well, there was very little information to the effect that he had been involved in that. All of this was something that was assumed by the neighbours, the neighbours thought, well -- it's our next door neighbours who must have attacked us, but I did not suspect him of anything and I said that there were no arguments to prove that and I told him not to burden himself with that type of thing. I told him to relax, which he accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you also ask him some questions sort of where the other Muslims were, where the 28th Division might have been?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Not in that sense. I did not mention the 28th Division, and I didn't know that there was a 28th division. I asked him whether he knew perhaps where the commanders of units -- well, the commanders who led Naser's units. There were several regional commanders depending on the localities involved, because they had been suspected of war crimes as well. So I cannot remember exactly now. He did mention something, and I wrote things down on a piece of paper. He gave me some information and that's it. I made a note. I said I had to make a note, nevertheless. Although only Nikolic had brought him, he was not with these people. Well, he said what he thought he knew. Possibly he could have mentioned the 28th Division, but now I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how -- how long, roughly, were you speaking to Mr. Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the information he provided you, did you have an opinion as to its reliability?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I had an opinion about that. I did not even ask about moment of units, I just asked about the names of persons who were suspects on the basis of that book. I wasn't interested in what units were involved and nobody had ordered me to do that, and I was not supposed to do that. But he talked spontaneously, so that was the information that was provided. He was brought there to my office after perhaps three or four hours, after having walked to Bratunac, and if there was a unit in some of the Srebrenica villages at the time of the action at Srebrenica, that was not relevant. Everyone was on the move, the Serb army and the Muslim army, and it was a question of minutes. I mean, that's my assumption. I don't know. I was not there on the field. So I did not take that as a piece of information that I would have to report to someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We probably need to slow down a little bit so we get the translation right.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. After speaking to Mr. Sinanovic, did you speak to the -- any of these other five, six Muslims that you had said had been brought to -- to your area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just looked at their IDs. And I put the same question, whether they knew. I mean, I asked every one of them whether they knew roughly where such and such people were. A few names, Rasunovic [phoen], Meholjic, Mandic. I knew them by heart, but I was leafing through the book. So if they knew anything, they spoke up. If not, then they would spontaneously talk about where it was that they went and from what village they set out from and how they reached Bratunac. Obviously they weren't soldiers but civilians, or at least some of them. That's probably the way it was, and I was taking notes about this, too. What they were saying, I thought I should write down on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I -- have I showed you the original notes that you have taken, that you took at the time when you were speaking to Mr. Sinanovic and these others?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you confirm that that was your handwriting and those were the notes you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let me skip a little bit now. After those prisoners left your area, did you again see Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on that day in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was it you saw Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The same place. Right there in front of the building of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What if anything had been going on in Bratunac that -- that afternoon and evening; anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the transport had already arrived of people who had surrendered or were taken prisoner. They were already there in Bratunac, lots of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say transport, what kind of transport?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: These were freight vehicles and buses. Trucks and buses, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who in particular were in these buses and trucks?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Adults. Men. Well, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see which direction they were coming in to Bratunac town from?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see where these buses and trucks went in Bratunac town?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw where they were parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was -- just roughly, where was that? We will get to a map a little later, I think.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The street that goes towards the elementary school Branko Radicevic in Bratunac. The street ends in front of the school, and then it forks off into different directions, so it is a straight street. It starts from the street of Gavrila Princip. That's what they call it nowadays and it goes to the building of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, do you remember the name of the elementary school back then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm sure that the name of the elementary school is Branko Radicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember what it was back then in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Before two elementary schools were established, there was one that was called Vuk Karadzic. And after two schools were established, one was called Vuk Karadzic, the old name that is, and the other one got the name of Branko Radicevic. Now, that always confused me a bit, where what school was, in terms of their names. That one was near the municipality, Branko Radicevic or Vuk Karadzic, it's near the municipality building, the specific school that I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll see if we can sort that out a bit later. Now, when you saw Mr. Beara outside, I guess it was near the office that evening, what if anything did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I've already said. I mean, I was the one to start the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that only a few people were brought in front of the police building. And that there are no results in terms of looking at the IDs, and then he says, "All right, what else?" And I said that I was worried because I went home around midday to change because it was very hot, and I saw that there were too many people who were prisoners in town, and too few soldiers - I mean Serb soldiers - and that probably the town is imperilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was his response to that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: All right, we'll have a look at that, but I hope that they will make it through the night and we will too, because I guess they're going to Kladanj tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing special. Quite simply he went out to see all of that. To see what the situation as outside in the street, that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you go with him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you -- where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: All the way to the school. From the command building, the building of the commander of the brigade, we walked along the street on foot, and he was just looking, he was looking at the vehicles and the guards. He didn't stop by anyone, simply he passed by and looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see any of these vehicles and trucks with Muslim men in them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what if anything did he say about them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, about them or to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's start with --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear your question, or rather I didn't hear the interpreter interpreting your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What if anything did he say about them to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I asked him why these people weren't leaving immediately, why were they standing there, and he aid that the transport had to be reorganised, that there were many people on the vehicles, and that it wasn't safe to transport them that way, and that the vehicles had to be returned. The vehicles that took the women and children, that they would be reorganised and they would go could Kladanj the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He said there were too many people on the vehicles for them to be transported that way?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, he said that there were too few vehicles in order to transport them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did he say anything to any of the Muslims in your presence?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. He didn't address anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The school, along the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Roughly what time of day was it now that you were in the -- in the -- going towards the school?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. We went back, we came to the school that is, and he went down towards the school, too, 10 or 15 metres, I wasn't with him, to the corner. He said it's not quite safe, but I think there won't be any problems. And then we returned up there. It didn't take very long because practically -- well, yes, at one moment we went to the stadium, too. He looked at the stadium. He looked at what the situation was. He looked from the gate. Whether he talked to someone or not, I could not hear because I stayed behind, but he returned soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to look into the stadium yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see anything -- anybody in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw a few vehicles next to the fence before the stadium, and also through the gate of the stadium. I could discern parts of buses and trucks because the fence prevented you from seeing that. So that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long was Mr. Beara over by the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly. I don't know, he stopped for a bit, a minute or two, I don't know whether he talked to someone or not, and not more than that. And then he came back and then we went down the street to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why didn't you go over to the stadium with him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were some soldiers in front of the gate. Quite simply, I stopped. I was talking behind him, a metre or two, for as long as he did whatever he wanted to do out there, to have a look, whatever. I didn't really feel like going. I was exhausted that day, so I was avoiding any kind of commotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslim men in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I did on the first vehicle. I didn't enter the stadium so I didn't see what was going on in the stadium. Just through the gate of the stadium I saw -- well, it was dusk, I wasn't sure. Now, was it the front part of the truck or the back or front of a bus, but I think I did see that there were people there on one of the vehicles. Now, who these people were, whether they were Muslims, too, or soldiers, I don't know. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And where did you go when you and Mr. Beara left the stadium area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, I was supposed to say that earlier on. We stopped at the stadium and then we returned to the school and to the police building, to in front of the police building. We talked slowly; we were on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you got back to the police building, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. He went into the yard of the command, and I went to my office to get things in order. It was dirty that day, nothing more than that. As for him, I didn't see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I had a map of Bratunac to help illustrate the walk. The one I have access to is the one that has the places marked. Given there was a slight confusion about the school, it may be better to give him the unmarked version. That unfortunately is in my office. But if the Defence doesn't object, we can show him the marked version. I mean, he knows Bratunac better than anyone, and it may not be prejudicial, but if there is a concern I can go to my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is -- the marked one, does it indicate the name of one or both schools?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So at that point, I suggest that he brings the clean one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Just on line -- or page 21, line 6, I thought the witness said that they walked slowly, and it says they talked slowly. I don't know if it's a big deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It will just take a minute or two for us to get the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's better we use the clean one, even though the witness familiar with Bratunac town. Unless there is the okay from the Defence teams. In which case we can use the one that he has now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's not, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's bring the clean one. In the meantime, if you can pass on to some other question, perhaps we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go back now to the time that you are in front of your office with the -- the Muslims. You have told us you interviewed Resid Sinanovic, I think you said in your office. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I only talked to him in the office. With the others outside, they didn't enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And where were the others when you spoke to them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The first one or two people while they were on the vehicle they got off to get some water, and outside in the shade underneath the window there were a few chairs and tree stumps and I was sitting there and taking notes on my knees. Handwritten notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you finished, do you know where Resid Sinanovic and these other Muslims were taken?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: First they were taken -- I mean these people who were together in the group, they were taken to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Because the guys who were the escorts asked where the school was, so they could take them there, and they returned with the vehicle five or six minutes later. They returned to the building, in front of the building. There were fewer of them then; two or three of these escorts, these guys who were escorting them. After that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, these -- these people that -- that took the Muslims to the school, how did they describe themselves in particular?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: As I started talking to these persons who were brought in, I asked for their IDs to see who they were and I asked for any ID. They were talking to a few of these military policemen from the platoon of the military police from Bratunac, and sort of we were specials, it was a sort of jargon, so I assumed that they were members of a special military unit or a special police. I don't know. At any rate, they were dressed the same way; new overalls. And one could see that perhaps they belonged to an elite unit, judging by their uniforms because our people were poorly dressed. It was along those lines. It wasn't that any one of them told me that they were members of this or that unit. I cannot claim that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me -- let me take you to see if this will help to refresh your recollection. Do you remember giving a statement on the 28th of August, 2003, to the Republika Srpska MUP at the Bratunac police station?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me read this to you to see if this is correct. I mean, earlier I -- you had a chance to read this -- this police statement, didn't you, in my office?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you tell me if it was correct or not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are two statements. I don't know which one you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this is the longest one with the most detail. It is the 28th of August. Let me just read you the short section to see if this is -- if this is right or if you want to clarify anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's page 5 in the -- in the English, in the middle of the first paragraph, and it's page -- ERN Y0033873, in the B/C/S original, near the bottom of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says, I believe, now referring to the -- to the Muslims, "We talked for about two hours and then a police patrol came to my office and said that Resid had spent too much time with me and that they were supposed to escort him to the elementary school for provisional accommodation. Since the policemen had represented themselves as special police, there could be no arguing with them because they were arrogant fellows 'specials,' and it was better not to get on their wrong side." Now, this -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So these guys called themselves special police?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: They called themselves "the specials." Not the special police. So I assume they were either the special police or a special platoon of the military, of the army. I wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know what the RS Special Police Unit was at the time, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I know what the unit of the military police looked like. As for the special police, I didn't look at the insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe the uniform that these police, these specials, let's call them the specials, as you have confirmed. What -- can you describe their uniforms a little better?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Overalls. Military overalls. They were camouflage overalls, and one could see that the fabric was new, that overalls were new, one could see very well. The belts that they had were not plain leather ones, no. They were the modern type ones and very few of our people had that. Our people had worn-out uniforms three years old, tops and trousers. That's what our people wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I now have that -- that map, and I don't know what number we want to give it, but we'll give it P2 -- if we could, for now I'm told, call it P2103, at page 272, that's Mr. Ruez's marked map. This will get a new number after he marks it up. And if you could give him that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- that pen and that map, and if we could gear up the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, you know, take your time. I know you saw this map in my office and -- but take your time to orient yourself with it. And when you do the first thing I want you to do is circle the buildings of the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. But take time to orient it. It's obviously shot at sort of an angle that can be tricky. You can turn it any way that makes sense to you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: May I use the pencil to draw on it or am I supposed only to point out without writing anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's work together on this, if you --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this -- is this suitable? This is the building, the building of the Kaolin factory. This is this building here. I'm circling it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Take the pen -- we're going to write on it. I don't want the whole factory, but can you circle the offices of the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Here. I have to do it with my left hand. I'm left handed. I don't know if I should turn it around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Definitely use your writing hand.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the front part of the building. And this is where premises were, official premises. The cafeteria was on the ground floor for the military, and this is where the offices of the command of the brigade were located, in this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Is that -- is that pen working?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is, okay. Sorry. It's just the ELMO. All right. You've drawn I guess a big oval around the office building. Can you put a 1, a clear 1 next to that, so we'll know what that is? You may need to mark hard so it comes through to us.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can you circle the place where your office was, what is known I believe as the military police building. And we can stay right there, ELMO people.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: This building here. This one here. This is where the reception desk is, and then the military police building is. And then my office was somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, you've marked your office, I guess, with something that looked like a 1, unfortunately. But let's ignore that and put a 2 on the roof of the military police building, that big rectangle you drew.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can you put a B1 where the first place where you saw Mr. Beara was, either on the night of the 12th or the morning of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, where was he when you met him that second time and took your walk into town? Just tell us where he was in relation to B1.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Closer to the reception desk or the gatehouse. Somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Put B2 next to that little dot, will you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if you could just visualise where you walked and before drawing, let's do it like a carpenter, let's look first and measure second. So can you just take your pen without writing it and just give us an outline of your walk and then we will mark it after that. Just go slowly from the headquarters to where you went into town and we'll mark it later.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: We started out from here, we took this street, and then went down this street called Gavrila Principa and turned left and we took this street and then we turned towards the stadium. I remained there and he went to the gate of went to the gate of the stadium and then came back and went to the school. This is the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you put a big circle around the school you're talking about, and just -- just put an S for "skola." Now, how do you know that school? What name do you know it by now? I know the name has changed a few times.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Called Branko Radicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you now just take a moment and draw in with your green pen that -- that route you just told us about? Just take your time and get it right.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks] Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: More or less. Okay. Now, on the way -- that line you've just drawn, I see that you go to the soccer field and then you go back and then down to the school. On your way back do you do the same route?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Same road except we didn't go to the playground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Or the -- the --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, we didn't go again to the playground; there was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say playground, you mean football pitch?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Stadium. I mean the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Everyone in Bratunac knows it as the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you roughly as you remember, put Xs where you remember seeing vehicles, buses and trucks that had Muslims in them? If you can.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The vehicles were parked with an interval of two to three metres. In -- in the street. So there was a column of vehicles with two to three metres between them. They filled up the street. So every two or three metres there would be a parked vehicle and then again two or three metres and then another parked vehicle, all the way up to the end of the street and the street ended in the front of the school, right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just put Xs to just roughly reflect that. It doesn't need to be the same number of vehicles as Xs, but Xs to give us an idea of where these vehicles were parked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was thinking also of using another there are, because at least from what I can see on -- on the monitor, I can barely decipher what -- of course if I look at the -- probably I will see it better, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we had that same problem with the colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, there were instances where the technicians actually did something and we could see the colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we blow it up a little bit? I think if we blow up to just have the route, we can see it. No, I mean down. Yeah, there we go. Okay. Right there, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you finish your Xs and ... Is that it? That's about the area where you saw the buses and trucks?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember roughly how many different buses and trucks you saw that had Muslims in them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: There could have been some 20 or so. I didn't count them, and I would hesitate to give you the exact figure, but they almost filled up the whole street. I don't know exactly how many buses can fit, but not -- maybe not the whole street, but from the bakery, there is a bakery here, all the way up to the school. This is the bakery. This is where the bakery is. Where the X is on the corner, this is where the bakery is, and then down. You said the street. Do you need to -- do you need for me to mark other locations with an X?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there any other locations where you saw numerous vehicles? Big vehicles with Muslims in them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: As I said earlier, that in front of the stadium gate I saw two or three vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't you put two or three Xs there, then.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you mentioned seeing something inside the stadium. How many vehicles did you see inside the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any vehicle in its entirety. I saw a portion of one vehicle, the front of it. I saw only half a metre of the front of that vehicle. I don't know whether that was a bus or a truck. It was dusk, and I stood by the stands at the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't you put a 0 where you saw part of that vehicle, if you can?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Here. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell whether there were any Muslim men inside the school?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What could you see?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I could see people on the windows. I'm now referring to the time when I saw them during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just asking you about that evening walk. What could you see during the evening walk? Did you see any Muslims at that school during your evening walk with Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw silhouettes, yes. They were in the classrooms on the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell -- did you -- what level of the classroom? I guess there is ground, at least a ground. I mean, how many -- how many levels does that school have?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: One or two storeys. I'm not sure exactly but there was on the upper storey. I don't know exactly how many storeys the building has, I think two, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Popovic around Bratunac on -- on that day that you saw Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see Mr. Popovic on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see him in Bratunac, do you remember seeing him at all during this time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I saw him one evening, either on the 10th or 11th in front of the brigade headquarters building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could he be more specific as to which Popovic he's referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say -- when I say -- when we say Popovic, can you tell us his -- who this person is?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Popovic. The security officer of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which corps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you say you think you saw him.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know what he looks like. I think I saw him and Mr. Beara one evening, but Mr. Beara didn't talk to me on that occasion. He didn't even see him nor did I approach him or anything. I just saw him. I saw a group of officers and I recognised him. Because he would come to see Nikolic frequently, and I could physically identify him easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you say "him" you mean Popovic the --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in this group of people, who did you see?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I just recognised Mr. Beara and Mr. Popovic. There were another two or three men, but that was after I had finished my dinner and gone back, and then I stood with the guards, not with the guards, but people manning the reception desk or the gatehouse, and they said the officers arrived, and I paid attention to them. I looked at them more carefully, and I recognised the two of them, and then there were two or three officers with them. I guess they were officers, but I'm not fully sure about that. I simply didn't see them that clearly, nor did I know them from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I just -- the last thing I want to do is show you these -- your -- your handwritten notes, and I think we can do that with the -- with the screen and the copies. If we could just go on e-court first to number 247. If we could blow that up briefly. Okay. Are these the notes regarding a person -- an interview of -- named Husic Mujo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the -- the next one, which is number 248. And if I could bring up the English as well as the B/C/S on this. We need to show the witness the B/C/S. Okay. Are these your notes of the interview with Resid Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could blow up the English bit -- a bit more so I can look at in the middle part of the notes. It looks like Mr. Sinanovic told you that -- it says, "In the first phase about 6.000 to 7.000 people crossed. Soldiers had priority. The majority of the soldiers crossed in the first wave." And then it says in parentheses, "(the plan to go from Pobudje towards Tuzla.)" And then, "This morning about 1.000 to 1500 armed men remained. About 6.000 to 7.000 remained in the spot where the shells landed." And then there is a little description. So when it says, "This morning about 1.000 to 1500 remained," do you know what day that was when he says, "This morning"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I hear -- I see here only two sentences of what you read out. Could you please scroll up with -- scroll down rather, with my text so that I can follow it? May I read this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. Take your time and take a look at that. And we can blow that up for him and kick off the English.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, this is good. Yes, yes, this is good. Can you scroll down a bit more? Thank you. Because I'm missing the bottom portion. All right. Now, would you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is a reference, when it says, "This morning about 1.000 to 1500 armed men remained," now you are clearly interviewing him on the 13th. Do you know when you wrote in "this morning," what you were referring to, what day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was on the 13th, because at the beginning of the text it says, "I started out this morning." Could I see the beginning of the text, please? Could we go back to the beginning? Because that was the most accurate information. I wrote down what he said. Yes, this is it. He says, "This morning I reported to the camp near Pobudje," which means that it was that morning on the 13th because this is how he started his story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Celanovic, I tell you I don't see any questions in your notes about the possibility of him being a war criminal, so you didn't write any notes about that part of your conversation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was a conversation, a verbal exchange. Because even before he was brought, there was actually no grounds for suspecting him in relation to anything. I just told him that I needed to speak to him, because he had heard what Captain Nikolic said, and I had to talk to him. There was nothing to write down, just the first name and the last name. I didn't know the other people, so I had to get more information from them, more personal particulars. And I asked him about other people. You can see based on the names that all of these people were mentioned, and you can see what kind of questions I put to him. Bekic, Golic, Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Understood. Let's go to the next one, which is number 249?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic said that the last bit of the witness gave, an important bit where he said the word "innocent," was missed out. Perhaps he could be asked if he mentioned the word "innocent" and in what context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you've heard Mr. Josse. Did you make use -- did you use the word "innocent"? And if you did, in what context did you use it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to which name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean Sinanovic or the other people mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sinanovic, apparently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for Sinanovic, yes. It is my position now that he was a decent and honest man. And following everything that happened nothing surfaced to indicate that he wronged anyone, committed a war crime against Serb civilians, soldiers or anything. He did not harm the Serbs in any way. This is still my opinion to this day. And that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just to -- or almost -- we're almost done, really. Let's go to the next one which I think I already said, 249. And if -- take a look. Does this indicate that you spoke briefly to Nasif Avdic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Munib Dedic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Aziz Husic? I think we need to ...

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I think if we can go to the last one of these. It says down at the bottom, "R.Z." for Hajrudin Begzadic. It says he was registered with a unit but did not take an active part. So what does that mean, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Hajrudin, I didn't see him on that day, but Husic claimed concerning Begzadic that he had been a member of a unit of Alija, nicknamed Kurta, and gave information about him because given that Aziz was from Brezovica, and this person, Hajrudin Izazic [phoen] from Brezovica was mentioned in the book as a person who was involved. So he provided information about where he was in the unit and where he was located. Nothing more. I made this note, and that has nothing to do with it. So just to -- just to reiterate, this person was not with me. And this is what Husic told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have two more documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead and then we will have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 250, this should be the last note. It will come up on this -- on this system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this indicate that you interviewed Hasib Ibisevic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just going briefly back to Resid Sinanovic, were you at some point shown a document indicating that he was -- he was alive on 15 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we could bring that up and that -- and should have a B/C/S version. The number is 2407, that's the English version. If we could bring them both up. But I think we can make this shorter by -- Do you remember being shown some medical documents by a lawyer named Veselin Londrovic who was representing Momir Nikolic at -- at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did he -- did he show you this -- this letter that we see the B/C/S version of?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just for the Court, you can see that this is a -- a reference from a -- a health centre sending a medical document from the hospital at Banja Koviljaca. Do you know where Banja Koviljaca is?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a town on the Drina River in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So if we could now go to -- let's go to the actual document itself, which is three pages down in this document. Page 3 in English, and page 3 in B/C/S. Okay. If we could blow that up a little bit to catch the 15 July segment of the English and the B/C/S which we see towards the bottom of the page. Okay. Now, in the English side the people that were trying to translate this were not able to being make out anything about "Resid" about three lines below where it says 15 July. Can you check out the B/C/S version about three lines down, does it say "Resid" there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Resid Sinanovic, both first and last name, written in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is you are understanding, just -- of what this document represents?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: It constitutes proof that Resid Sinanovic has been registered or entered in this document. If it's a hospital document, then that he was in the hospital. I looked at this document before, and I know that this is part of the medical centre's protocol records in Banja Koviljaca, meaning that he was receiving treatment or was there for treatment that day, since he's been registered in this particular form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And where -- where is Banja Koviljaca?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already told us, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Banja Koviljaca, to be more specific, is a town across from the town of Bijeljina. It is further away from Zvornik. It's not precisely opposite from Bijeljina, but it is more or less on the other side of the river Drina in the Republic of Serbia. It is 40 or 50 kilometres from Zvornik, down river from the Drina on the right bank of the river Drina in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The letter from -- the letter from a doctor says from Loznica, the health centre from Loznica. Do you know whether this medical record is coming from a health centre in Loznica or Banja Koviljaca?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The medical centre has a business, an organisational seat in Loznica. The health centre, or whatever it's called, in Banja Koviljaca is territorially part of that centre. Legally it's part of the Milenko Marin centre from Loznica, even though it is not physically in the same place. It is as if a company had a branch in another place. There is for example one in Amsterdam and one in The Hague. I mean, it's the same way. So part of the medical centre in Loznica, is this particular unit in Banja Koviljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What town is across the river from Loznica in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that Bijeljina is the closest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Kozluk, well, Kozluk, I even forgot that it was a town. It's a very small place. Kozluk is a settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Witness, we will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand you're finished, but I see you standing up again, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am reminded the witness needs to sign and date the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see him do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]. [Interpretation] What was the date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Today is the 31st of January. Okay. Mr. Zivanovic will go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You provided a statement before, actually you gave a number of statements at the police station in Bratunac, and to the Tribunal investigators?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read just one sentence from that statement that you provided at the Bratunac police station, and then after that I'm going to put a question to you. The sentence reads, "I know from speaking with military policemen of the Bratunac Brigade that they participated as an escort to the convoy or convoys and that the hand-over of the vehicles with the prisoners was carried out at the border between the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigade's areas of responsibility." My question is, on that occasion did they tell you or mention that this was done at a place called Vidikovac?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Only the area the responsibility was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't mention any location at all?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if -- or until when did you stay in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I think until the 14th of December, 1995. Just before the signing of the Dayton Accords, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me one more thing. I saw from your previous statements that amongst other things as part of your duties you compiled data on attacks on the Serbian villages around Bratunac and Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if you know what happened after that? With that material that you had compiled with the documents, the material, the statements and all of that, did that stay at the Bratunac Brigade or not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it stayed or a part of it stayed. I have to give you a broader answer, if you permit me. I compiled the material upon orders of the commander in cooperation with the representatives of the commission for the investigation of war crimes of Republika Srpska and Yugoslavia, so they were sent to me by the commander as a person who was skilled in compiling data and getting statements and so on. So I was authorised by the commander to take statements from civilians. Whatever I compiled I would hand over to the representatives of those two commissions. They actually took most of the statements to the centre for the investigation of war crimes in Yugoslavia. Maybe I'm not naming the -- the commission properly. Luka [phoen] Ivanisevic was the authorised person. I remember quite well he was authorised by Biljana Plavsic to come to the command of the brigade, and that he was authorised to investigate into Republika Srpska. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you can remember, can you tell me if there were many cases reported of attacks on Serbian villages around Bratunac and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Could your question be a little more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your work on this matter that we just talked about, did you have information from people that you took the various statements from about how many attacks there were on Serbian villages? Did this occur once, several times, were there attacks on one village or on several villages? This is my question.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. There were I a tacks on all Serbian villages in the area of the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean? How many of them are there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many of them there are, 50, 60. Well, not all. The villages that were below Bratunac, only Polje [phoen] and Slapasnica were not attacked. All the other villages were attacked, Kravica, Jezestica, Bijelovac, and so on. Each village as attacked by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you found out what the consequences of these attacks were?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. There were many soldiers and civilians killed in each attack and property was destroyed. There was looting and burning of Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say soldiers and civilians, do you mean Serb soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm thinking of Serb soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion did you find out who carried out the attacks where the attackers were coming from, which direction were they coming from, those who attacked the villages?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I did have some information because the survivors could always identify someone from the other side. There was fighting, they would see someone. Mostly these are people from two towns who knew each other from before the war. They would recognise someone and were able to indicate by first and last name who the persons were whom they recognised who were in the attack. That caused these consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did they indicate from which direction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you are moving too fast, both of you. Please allow a short pause between question and answer. All right? Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions. Could you please tell me if you had information as to the direction from which those attackers had come from?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I did have information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to answer. Each village was defended to a certain degree, so they came from the other side of the line from the direction of Srebrenica, from the Srebrenica villages, there was some kind of line between Bratunac and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know how long these attacks lasted? I don't mean in the sense of how long they lasted in hours and minutes, but I mean the length, the period over which the attacks happened, was it months, weeks, years?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The most intense attacks were during 1992. But they continued later. Practically until the end of the war there were incursions into Serbian villages and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. Could you please tell me if you received information after the attacks about where the attackers withdrew, which direction did they withdraw towards?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Towards Srebrenica, the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this was during the period that Srebrenica was a protected zone?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. I have Ms. Nikolic is going next? I have this order indicated to me. First Mr. Zivanovic, second Ms. Nikolic, third the Borovcanin Defence, fifth Madam Fauveau, sixth is -- fifth is the Gvero Defence, next is Mr. Haynes or Mr. Sarapa, and last is the Beara team.
